02 Assignment Part 1 · Select

The visualization under review

I choose Evelina Gabasova’s Episode IV network to analyze and revise, which is a rich public example: it is technically ambitious, immediately recognizable, and complex enough to support a meaningful redesign rather than a cosmetic restyle.

Original work

The Star Wars social network

Creator
Evelina Gabasova
Published

Form

Data

Open the original article ↗ Open the archived dataset ↗ Open the original GitHub repository ↗

Original Design Description

In this original visualization, nodes are denoted as screenplay characters; a link is created when two characters speak within the same screenplay scene; its weight counts those shared speaking scenes. Node size represents the number of scenes attributed to a character. The published “all characters” version supplements R2-D2 and Chewbacca with mention-based approximations, which is an important methodological caveat for interpretation.

03 Assignment Part 2 · Analyze

Message, audience, and intended tasks

01 / Message

Reveal the social structure of the story

The visualization communicates which characters are prominent and connected, which pairs interact frequently, and how the cast separates into narrative groups. Viewers should notice Luke’s central position, the dense hero group, Imperial and Rebel-pilot clusters, and peripheral characters with few or weak connections.

02 / Audience

Fans first; visualization readers second

Its primary audience is general Star Wars fans curious about the film from a quantitative perspective. A secondary audience includes readers interested in data visualization, digital humanities, and introductory network analysis. Major character familiarity helps, but advanced statistics are not required.

03 / Tasks

Explore adjacency, prominence, and structure

  • Compare node sizes to identify prominent characters.
  • Determine whether two characters are connected.
  • Compare relationship frequency through link thickness.
  • Find central, peripheral, or bridging characters.
  • Recognize clusters and form an overview of network structure.
  • Hover for names and drag nodes to inspect crowded areas.

04 Assignment Part 3 · Critique

What works—and what the hairball hides

Author's Note: the original visualization succeeds as an overview, but its encoding and interaction design make precise comparison and methodological interpretation unnecessarily difficult. After careful consideration, I decided to use four new visualizations to together do the task.

2 Strengths

The relationship model is intuitive

What works: nodes and links match the familiar mental model of a social network.

Why it matters: fans can quickly determine whether characters are connected without learning a specialized chart grammar.

Author creates a comprehensive and compact overview

What works: the view includes the broad Episode IV cast while using size and link width to encode two quantitative attributes.

Why it matters: it exposes major characters, minor groups, and network shape in one space-efficient display.

4 Weaknesses / Opportunities

Labels and legends do not define the visual encodings

Problem: the chart does not visibly define a scene, interaction, node-size scale, link-width scale, or the special handling of non-speaking characters.

Why it matters: the intended audience can mistake co-occurrence frequency for screen time or emotional closeness, so the marks and channels become semantically ambiguous.

Improvement: every redesigned view now names its measure, denominator, and unit; tooltips expose exact values, while the method note and report document provenance and limitations.

Marks, position, and visual hierarchy create a hairball

Problem: dozens of nodes, labels, and crossing links compete for the same space; force-directed position is visually prominent even though distance has no quantitative scale.

Why it matters: occlusion and weak hierarchy make tracing a relationship, locating a bridge, or identifying a cluster slow and error-prone.

Improvement: the interactive network limits scope to eight declared principal characters, uses direct labels, and supports dragging, hover details, and linked focus across all four views.

Link width is ineffective for precise comparison

Problem: link widths are unaligned, lack tick marks or an axis, and must be compared across different orientations; color does not provide a redundant quantitative cue.

Why it matters: viewers cannot reliably rank close values, retrieve an exact pair count, or locate the strongest and weakest relationships.

Improvement: the adjacency matrix adds aligned cells, a high-contrast sequential luminance scale, exact numbers, and sortable order for lookup, extrema, and cluster tasks.

The design does not support the full message or task set

Problem: one aggregate network shows neither each character’s share of appearances nor when and where scenes occur; shape, color, and position encode little narrative context.

Why it matters: the audience can inspect adjacency but cannot compare prominence as a composition or connect relationships to story space and sequence.

Improvement: the treemap supplies a valid part-to-whole view, while the circular scene-space diagram restores screenplay order, location categories, and details on demand.

05 Assignment Part 4 · Redesign

Revised: Four-View Dashboard

Author's Note: my redesign intentionally focuses on eight principal characters to add clarity. Notice that every view uses the same screenplay-derived presence definition and the same visual identity system.

The focus set

Eight principal characters

Author's Note: character colors remain stable across the node-link network, adjacency matrix, treemap, and radial layout.

Linked selection

Select a node, cell, tile, or name to focus

View 01

A much clearer and interactive relationship network

This view directly revises the original network while reducing clutter to eight principal characters. Drag any node to reorganize the layout, hover over a node or link for exact scene counts, and select a character or pair to coordinate every view. Node area encodes individual scene presence; link width encodes pairwise co-presence.

Node size = Number of scenes Link width = Number of shared scenes

View 02

An adjacency matrix for more precise comparison

I add this matrix because the original network’s unaligned link widths do not support reliable quantitative comparison. The dataset contains all 28 unique pairs among the eight characters; each symmetric off-diagonal cell reports that pair’s number of shared screenplay scenes. A stronger light-to-dark scale, exact labels, and sorting make pair lookup, ranking, extrema, and cluster detection substantially more precise.

View 03

A treemap of character-scene appearances

I add this treemap because connectivity and individual narrative presence answer different questions. Area shows each character’s share of the 536 scene appearances accumulated by the eight selected characters. This additive denominator makes the view a valid part-to-whole comparison and avoids falsely claiming that overlapping character appearances partition the film’s runtime.

share = character scenes ÷ sum of all eight characters’ scenes

Narrative geography

Four operational spaces

Author's Note: since the whole story took place across four broad narrative spaces, I am also interested in creating a space-scene-character mapping. Therefore, scene headings are coded into four mutually exclusive macro-locations. Ship interiors and general space scenes form “Outer Space / Spacecraft.” I checked the January 15, 1976 revised fourth-draft screenplay used for the analysis; ambiguous cases follow the written scene heading and are disclosed as a limitation.

Tatooine

Desert, homestead, canyons, Mos Eisley, and Docking Bay 94.

Death Star

Station interiors, surface, gun emplacements, and trench scenes.

Yavin IV

Massassi temple, briefing room, war room, and Rebel hangars.

Outer Space / Spacecraft

Starships, hyperspace, fighter cockpits, and general space.

View 04

A radial scene-to-space map

I add this circular view because the aggregate network cannot show story order or setting. The outer circle places all 300 relevant screenplay scenes in narrative order; the segmented inner circle encodes the four operational spaces. Curved, location-colored bundles connect each scene to its space, while scene-dot size reports how many principal characters are present. Character filtering reveals where an individual narrative path concentrates or crosses between spaces.

06 Assignment Part 5 · Explain

Design Decisions Explanation

01

Reduce clutter while preserving the relationship model

What changed: I retained eight declared principal characters, fixed a readable starting layout, added direct labels, and made every node draggable with node and link tooltips.

Why: the original node-link metaphor is intuitive, so it should be improved rather than discarded.

Problem addressed: overlapping marks, crossings, weak hierarchy, and inaccessible exact values in the original hairball.

Improvement: viewers can trace neighborhoods, rearrange occluded relationships, and retrieve exact individual or pairwise scene counts while retaining a recognizable overview.

02

Add a matrix for defensible quantitative comparison

What changed: I added an 8 × 8 adjacency matrix with exact labels, high-contrast ordered luminance, and three meaningful sort orders.

Why: position in aligned rows and columns supports more accurate comparison than judging unaligned link widths.

Problem addressed: the original makes close relationship strengths difficult to rank and provides no reliable lookup scale.

Improvement: viewers can identify maxima, compare any pair, expose clusters, and verify the same relationship shown in the network.

03

Separate individual presence from connectivity

What changed: I added a treemap whose area represents each character’s share of 536 total character-scene appearances among the selected eight.

Why: frequent appearance and network centrality are related but distinct ideas that should not be compressed into one mark.

Problem addressed: the original provides little compositional context and encourages node size to carry too much interpretive weight.

Improvement: the additive denominator supports a valid part-to-whole task and lets viewers compare narrative presence against relationship structure.

04

Restore story order and narrative space

What changed: I placed relevant scenes in screenplay order on an outer circle, divided an inner circle into four location sectors, and bundled colored scene-to-space connections.

Why: aggregate social ties cannot explain where a scene occurs or how a character’s path moves through the story.

Problem addressed: missing chronology, setting, and details-on-demand in the original visualization.

Improvement: viewers can follow spatial concentration, filter a character’s scenes, and connect sequence and setting without confusing either with relationship strength.

Original versus redesign

The original remains more comprehensive because it includes minor characters, but the redesigned dashboard makes adjacency, exact pair comparison, part-to-whole presence, and scene-location exploration substantially easier. The trade-offs are deliberate: filtering removes minor-character context; treemap area is less precise than a bar; and four macro-locations simplify ambiguous settings. These limitations are documented so the broader task coverage does not overstate the screenplay-derived evidence.

07 Submission Report

Full Visualization Critique and Design Report

A focused report connecting the original visualization, critique, redesign decisions, comparison, limitations, figures, and sources.

Required report · 500–800 words

Visualization Critique and Redesign

Original visualization and context

Evelina Gabasova’s Episode IV: A New Hope social network is a force-directed, weighted node-link visualization derived from screenplay data. Nodes represent characters; an edge connects two characters when they speak within the same scene. Node size encodes the number of scenes attributed to a character, and link width encodes shared speaking scenes. The published “all characters” version supplements R2-D2 and Chewbacca through mention-based data because they do not speak conventional dialogue. The visualization’s intended message is that screenplay interaction reveals prominence, recurring relationships, and narrative groups. Its primary audience is Star Wars fans seeking a quantitative interpretation, with visualization and digital-humanities readers as a secondary audience. Intended tasks include finding prominent or peripheral characters, determining whether a pair connects, comparing relationship frequency, identifying bridges, and recognizing clusters.

Critical evaluation

Two strengths make the original a productive starting point. First, nodes and links match an intuitive social-network model: adjacency and broad topology can be understood without specialized statistical knowledge. Second, the compact overview includes a wide cast and uses two quantitative channels, making Luke and the densely connected hero group visually salient. The familiar character names also lower the entry barrier for a general audience and make the network inviting to explore.

Four weaknesses limit effectiveness. The chart does not visibly define “interaction,” scene segmentation, node size, link width, or the treatment of non-speaking characters; viewers may therefore confuse co-occurrence with screen time or emotional closeness. Numerous marks, crossing edges, and labels create a hairball with weak visual hierarchy, while force-directed distance appears meaningful despite having no quantitative scale. Link width is also difficult to compare across orientations because it lacks alignment, ticks, or exact labels; width is a less accurate comparison channel than aligned position or luminance. Node area similarly requires a legend or direct value to support precise magnitude judgments. Finally, the aggregate network cannot show the composition of character presence, screenplay order, or the settings where scenes occur. These are not aesthetic objections: they directly obstruct lookup, comparison, clustering, and narrative-context tasks identified for the intended audience.

Redesign rationale

The redesign coordinates four complementary D3 views. First, the node-link view retains the original’s intuitive structure but limits scope to eight declared principal characters. A stable starting layout, direct labels, dragging, linked highlighting, and node and edge tooltips reduce clutter while preserving exploratory topology. Second, an 8 × 8 adjacency matrix represents all 28 unique pairs using aligned cells, exact counts, sortable order, and a high-contrast sequential scale. This makes maxima, close values, and clusters more defensible than comparisons based only on link width. The two views are intentionally redundant: the network supports topology and paths, whereas the matrix supports exact pairwise comparison. Linked selection preserves their relationship.

Third, a treemap separates individual presence from connectivity. Area encodes each character’s share of 536 character-scene appearances accumulated by the selected eight. This is a valid additive whole; it deliberately does not claim that overlapping character appearances partition film runtime. Fourth, a circular scene-space view adds context absent from the original. Its outer circle orders 300 relevant scenes, its segmented inner circle identifies Tatooine, the Death Star, Yavin IV, and Outer Space/Spacecraft, and bundled colored curves connect every scene to its coded setting. Filtering exposes an individual character’s spatial path. Coordinated selection across all views supplies details on demand without permanently increasing clutter.

Original versus redesign, trade-offs, and limitations

The dashboard makes exact pair lookup, relationship ranking, character focusing, part-to-whole comparison, and scene-location exploration easier than the original. It also distinguishes connectivity, individual presence, sequence, and setting instead of asking one diagram to represent all four concepts. The main trade-off is scope: minor characters are removed, so the original remains better for cast completeness. Treemap area is less precise than a sorted bar, and four macro-locations simplify some ship and battle settings. Most importantly, the source is the January 15, 1976 revised fourth draft, not finished-film timing. Scene presence is inferred from speaker cues and action text, and draft or rapidly cross-cut scenes may differ from the released movie. The dashboard labels these limits to prevent stronger claims than the data supports. The four-view approach also increases learning cost and page length, but short reading guides, consistent character colors, direct labels, and coordinated interaction mitigate that cost while keeping each view responsible for a clearly stated analytical task.
